title: Choose the right format
html:
Start with a vacancy and an evidence file

By the end of the course, you will have a tailored CV, a one-page cover letter, and a checked set of files for one real vacancy. Keep the job ad and a private evidence file open while you work. You can use paid work, placements, school projects, community work, and volunteering as sources of evidence.

Read the employer’s instructions first

  1. Save the full posting. Record the job title, reference, deadline, language, file types, naming rules, upload fields, and any requested documents.
  2. Identify the document type. For most jobs, a CV or résumé is a concise record of relevant qualifications and results. An academic CV often includes publications, teaching, research, grants, and presentations. Use the document the vacancy requests.
  3. Choose a readable base format. Use a single-column layout with selectable text, familiar headings, consistent dates, and the latest entry first within each section. Follow a specified template if one is provided.
  4. Set your editing sequence. Match evidence to the job first. Draft the CV next. Write the letter once you know which examples deserve more explanation. Check the two files together.

Adapt to the job market

Hiring contextPractical starting point
United States and CanadaUse a targeted résumé for most jobs. Omit the photo and personal details such as date of birth and marital status in a standard application.
United KingdomEmployers often ask for a CV. Use contact details and relevant evidence. The National Careers Service advises leaving out age, date of birth, marital status, and nationality.
EU and EuropassUse Europass when requested. Check the country and employer’s guidance on layout and photographs. Use clear dates and select only relevant entries.
Cambodia and international employersRead the employer’s instructions for language, photo, documents, and submission. For an English application without a prescribed format, start with a concise, text-first CV and a one-page letter. Share sensitive documents only through a verified channel when genuinely required.

Know what each document does

The CV lets a reader locate evidence quickly. The letter shows why you chose this role and explains one or two examples in greater depth. Use the same dates, titles, and figures in both. For common early-career applications, aim for one page of CV evidence if it fits comfortably. Use a second page when relevant detail warrants it and the vacancy permits. Keep the letter to one page unless instructed otherwise.

Practice · Set up your workspace

Create a folder with your job posting, a private evidence sheet, and two draft documents. Write down the employer’s requirements for format and attachments. If the instructions only say “Send your CV and cover letter,” note that your working plan is a text-first CV and a one-page letter, with the final file format checked before submitting.

Check your work. You should be able to name the role, the employer, the deadline or where to find it, and exactly what you must send. This is the intake sheet you will use in Lesson 2.

title: Read the vacancy and map your evidence
html:
Turn the job advert into a plan

A tailored application is easier to write once you know what the employer needs to see. Our practice vacancy is fictional. Mekong Learning Hub is hiring a Learning Operations Coordinator (MLH-026) to schedule classes, maintain accurate attendance records, and communicate with instructors in Khmer and English. Experience with a learning platform is desirable. The advert asks for an English CV and cover letter.

Build an evidence map

  1. Underline the tasks. Copy brief phrases such as “schedule classes” and “maintain accurate attendance records.” These become the left column of your map.
  2. Rank the requirements. Mark essentials, desirable skills, and administrative instructions. Essentials guide your strongest CV bullets and letter examples. Instructions guide what and how you submit.
  3. Find a specific example. Search your experience for the task, tools, dates, scope, and result. Check your records or ask yourself how you would explain the claim in an interview.
  4. Choose a placement. Put brief factual evidence in the CV. Use the letter to explain how one example happened and why it matters to this employer.

Decide what to feature

RequirementDara’s verified example in the scenarioPlacement
Schedule classesCoordinated 24 sessions with six instructors during one term.First experience bullet. Letter paragraph 2 explains the process.
Maintain attendance recordsTested a shared spreadsheet checklist. Weekly reconciliation took 7 minutes instead of 18 in the timed trial.Second bullet. Letter paragraph 3 explains the accuracy check.
Communicate in Khmer and EnglishSent bilingual reminders for schedule and room changes.Experience bullet and language entry. Mention in the letter if relevant.
Learning platform experienceUsed shared spreadsheets and calendars. Has not used the employer’s platform.List the tools used. Explain the related workflow if the gap is material.

Research one reason to apply

Look for a concrete detail in the job ad or an official employer page. Record what you saw, where, and why it matters to the role. In the practice advert, the hub runs evening English classes for working adults. Dara connects that fact to reliable schedules and clear updates for learners planning around work. One researched reason shows the employer why this opportunity makes sense for you.

Practice · Map three requirements

Use the worksheet at the end of the course. Write three requirements from your own vacancy, with a fact you can support and the place it belongs. Circle the two strongest examples for the letter. Mark a gap honestly, then identify related experience you can explain in an interview.

Check your work. A line such as “Good at reports” is hard to verify. “Reviewed weekly attendance records for missing entries and sent a summary to tutors” gives a reader a task, purpose, and audience. If you have no defensible figure, keep the specific action and outcome.

title: Put CV sections in the right order
html:
Give the reader a clear path through your CV

Use the order below when your work or project experience is the strongest evidence. Keep role, organisation, dates, and results together. Put your strongest relevant bullets first within each entry.

  1. Name and contact. Place these first so a recruiter can identify and reach you. Use a professional email and phone number with country code for international hiring. Add your city and a current professional link only when useful.
  2. Profile, when it earns space. Use two or three lines naming your area of work and strongest relevant evidence. Put it near the top to give context. Omit it if it adds only adjectives or repeats your first bullet.
  3. Relevant experience. Show role, organisation, location if helpful, and dates. Include two to four focused bullets for your most relevant roles. Employers can see how and when you used the skills listed later.
  4. Education and training. Give the qualification, institution, and completion date or expected completion. Move education above experience if a recent qualification is required or is your strongest evidence.
  5. Skills, languages, and optional sections. Name tools or languages you can demonstrate. Put a required licence or certification near the top. Add relevant projects or volunteering when they fill an evidence gap.

Worked CV · Dara Sok

DARA SOK

Phnom Penh, Cambodia · dara.sok@example.com · [phone with country code]

Profile

Learning operations assistant with experience scheduling English classes, maintaining attendance records, and coordinating instructor updates in Khmer and English.

Relevant experience

Programme Assistant (part-time) · Riverbank Community Centre, Phnom Penh
Feb 2025 – Oct 2026

  • Coordinated 24 sessions across six instructors in one term using a shared calendar. Confirmed room and timetable changes with instructors before class.
  • Introduced a verification checklist in Google Sheets. Cut weekly attendance reconciliation from 18 to 7 minutes in a timed trial.
  • Sent Khmer and English reminders to instructors about schedule and room changes.

Volunteer Registration Assistant · Reading Together Phnom Penh
Jun 2024 – Jan 2025

  • Checked participant sign-in sheets and flagged incomplete records to the event lead before weekly reporting.

Education

Diploma in Business Administration · Riverside College, Phnom Penh · 2024

Skills and languages

Google Sheets (filters, data validation) · Shared calendars · Khmer (native) · English (working proficiency)

Practice · Choose your order

Write your proposed headings in order. If you are a recent graduate applying for a job requiring your qualification, try Contact → Education → Relevant Projects → Experience → Skills. If you are changing careers, try Contact → Targeted Profile → Relevant Experience → Additional Experience → Training → Skills. Keep dates visible in either version.

Check your work. Point to the first piece of proof an employer will see for the job’s top requirement. If it sits near the bottom, move the relevant section or bullet higher.

title: Write and tailor evidence bullets
html:
Turn duties into evidence

A duty describes what your role involved. An evidence bullet shows a specific action, the setting or scale, and what happened. The reader can then compare your contribution with the vacancy.

Write one bullet in three passes

  1. Choose an accurate action. Start with a verb that matches your contribution. Use “coordinated,” “analysed,” “prepared,” or “verified” where true. Use “supported” when another person led the work.
  2. Add context. Name the object, tool, audience, frequency, or scale. “Maintained an attendance spreadsheet for six instructors” is stronger than “worked with data.”
  3. Add the result or purpose. Specify what changed or what the work enabled. If you measured it, include the baseline, result, and scope when they matter. If you did not measure it, name the completed output or practical purpose.

Measured example. “Introduced a verification checklist in Google Sheets. Cut weekly attendance reconciliation from 18 to 7 minutes in a timed trial.” The scope signals that the result came from a trial.

Unmeasured example. “Checked participant sign-in sheets and flagged incomplete records to the event lead before weekly reporting.” The action, timing, and intended use provide evidence even without a metric.

Tailor language and check reading order

  1. Use the vacancy’s terms when they match your experience. If the employer says “attendance reporting,” use that phrase where it describes your work. Add the full form of a relevant abbreviation on first use when the reader may be unfamiliar with it.
  2. Keep headings plain and recognisable, such as Experience, Education, and Skills. Place vital contact details in the main document body. Avoid using icons, photographs, or graphical skill bars to carry essential information.
  3. Export the file type the employer requests. For a PDF, highlight the text, then copy it to a plain-text editor. Check the order of names, dates, headings, and bullets. This is a basic text and reading-order check. Employer systems vary.
  4. Read a printed or mobile preview. Look for cramped text, invisible links, unexpected page breaks, and headings left alone at the bottom of a page.

Make career changes and gaps easy to read

Move evidence of transferable work forward. A retail shift lead moving into learning operations could show rota planning, updated instructions, and record checks. Keep the original job title. Use a brief, truthful dated entry for a material gap when it clarifies the timeline and you choose to disclose it. Relevant learning or volunteering can be listed with its own dates.

Practice · Rewrite three bullets

Choose one real duty, one project, and one collaboration example. Write each using action, context, and result or purpose. Underline every number. Be ready to explain where it came from. Circle the one bullet that most closely matches your job advert and move it to the top of its entry.

Check your work. “Chased attendance every week” could become “Reviewed weekly attendance sheets and followed up on missing entries before monthly reports were compiled.” Add a number only if your records support it. Clear verbs and concrete scope matter more than forceful wording.

title: Plan the letter and write the opening
html:
Set up the letter so it is easy to route and read

Use the same name and contact details as the CV. A one-page attachment usually starts with your contact details, the date, the recipient or hiring team, and the organisation. Add the job title and reference in the subject when useful. Use the portal’s text format when the employer asks you to paste the letter into a field.

Build a clear opening

  1. Address the reader appropriately. Use the verified name if you know it. “Dear Hiring Team,” works when the recipient is unknown. Check names and titles carefully.
  2. Name the application immediately. Write the exact role and reference. This helps the recipient route your application and recognise which vacancy you mean.
  3. Connect one employer detail to the work. Use a fact you can verify in the advert or an official source. Connect it to something you can contribute. This gives the paragraph a clear reason for being specific to the employer.
I am applying for the Learning Operations Coordinator role (MLH-026). Your evening English programme serves adults who plan classes around work. My experience coordinating class schedules and keeping attendance records would help your instructors and learners get timely, reliable information.

Why this opening works. The first sentence identifies the role. The second shows that Dara understands who the programme serves. The third names relevant contributions and their purpose.

Plan each paragraph before drafting

ParagraphReader’s questionWrite this
1 · Purpose and fitWhich vacancy, and why here?The exact role, an employer detail, and a short link to your relevant experience.
2 · Strongest evidenceCan this candidate do the core work?A specific example with action, context, result or purpose, and a sentence about relevance.
3 · Additional evidenceWhat else supports the fit?A different essential skill or a short explanation of transferable experience. Combine with paragraph 2 if one example is enough.
4 · CloseWhat happens next?Thank the reader, invite a discussion, and use a professional closing and your name.

Use plain, confident language

Write about actions in the first person. Keep sentences direct and polite. Use the employer’s name and terms accurately. “I coordinated changes with instructors using a shared calendar” gives a reader a specific action. Replace expressions such as “I am the perfect candidate” with evidence that a recruiter can evaluate.

Practice · Draft two opening sentences

Use this scaffold, then read your draft aloud. “I am applying for [exact role, reference]. Your [verified activity or need] interests me because [specific connection to my evidence or contribution].” Add a third sentence if the connection needs more room.

Check your work. Try replacing the employer name with a different organisation. If every sentence still works, add a fact that ties the letter to this role. Check the fact against the source before submitting.

UK covering letter guidance · Europass cover letter guidance

title: Develop the body and close
html:
Make each paragraph do a different job

Use the middle paragraphs to show how you worked and what the employer can expect from you. A strong paragraph begins with one point, develops it with a real example, and connects the example to the role.

Explain the work behind the CV bullet

In paragraph 2, Dara explains how the timetable was managed. In paragraph 3, Dara explains how a spreadsheet checklist helped catch missing records. Both paragraphs use evidence on the CV, but the letter adds the sequence and reasoning. A closing paragraph works best after that evidence because the reader already has a reason to consider an interview.

Adapt when you are changing careers

Use a short bridge from the previous setting to the new one. For example, “As a retail shift lead, I managed a weekly rota for 12 colleagues and confirmed shift changes directly. That work taught me how to keep a schedule current when several people depend on it. I would apply the same approach to instructor timetables.” Keep the specific experience, explain the shared skill, and name the new application of it.

Practice · Write a body paragraph and close

Choose the top requirement in your map. Draft three or four sentences that name a relevant situation, explain your action, and tie the result or purpose to the job. Add a second example only if it proves something different. End with a short thank-you and an invitation to discuss your fit.

Check your work. Highlight one claim in each paragraph. If a paragraph contains three unrelated claims, give the strongest one a clear example and save the others for the CV or interview.

Worked cover letter · Dara Sok

Dara Sok · Phnom Penh, Cambodia · dara.sok@example.com
20 November 2026
Hiring Team · Mekong Learning Hub

Re: Learning Operations Coordinator (MLH-026)

Dear Hiring Team,

I am applying for the Learning Operations Coordinator role (MLH-026). Your evening English programme serves adults who plan classes around work. My experience coordinating class schedules and keeping attendance records would help your instructors and learners get timely, reliable information.

At Riverbank Community Centre, I coordinated 24 sessions across six instructors during one term. I used a shared calendar, checked room changes and sent updates in Khmer and English before class. I would bring the same approach to keeping your evening timetable current when instructors or rooms change.

I also tested a Google Sheets checklist that made missing attendance entries easier to spot. In a timed trial, I completed weekly reconciliation in 7 minutes, down from 18. A short verification routine like this would help me keep your records current and flag entries that need follow-up.

Thank you for considering my application. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how I can support your evening classes and help instructors keep accurate records.

Kind regards,
Dara Sok

What makes the four paragraphs professional?

  1. Opening. The exact title and reference make the application identifiable. The evening programme detail gives the employer a relevant reason for Dara’s interest.
  2. First evidence. The measurable scope and sequence make the scheduling experience credible. The last sentence makes the connection explicit.
  3. Second evidence. The trial result is bounded and traceable. The explanation adds a distinct record-checking example.
  4. Close. The request is courteous and specific. The paragraph adds no new claims for a reader to verify.

title: Audit and submit both documents
html:
Run four checks before submitting

Finish the application with a separate review pass. Open the exported documents you will actually submit. Use the advert as a checklist and read each file at normal size.

  1. Match. Verify the employer’s name, role, reference, language, deadline and time zone, file types, and required attachments. Confirm that the CV puts the strongest relevant evidence near the top.
  2. Accuracy. Compare dates, job titles, and figures between documents. Check names and spelling. Test the email address, phone number, and links. Review the PDF or document for comments, tracked changes, placeholder text, and outdated details.
  3. Readability. Check page breaks, font size, spacing, and reading order. Where PDF is permitted, confirm that text is selectable. If the application portal extracts information into fields, review and correct the fields before submitting.
  4. Delivery. Name the files clearly, for example Dara-Sok-CV.pdf and Dara-Sok-Cover-Letter-MLH-026.pdf. Follow any required naming pattern. Verify the recipient or portal and open the final attachments one more time.

Submit through the requested channel

Some employers use an online form and others ask for an email. If the letter is attached, write a short email. If the employer requests the letter in the body, use your letter there and attach only the requested files. For a portal, review any preview and save the confirmation or application number.

Subject: Application for Learning Operations Coordinator (MLH-026) | Dara Sok

Dear Hiring Team,

I am applying for the Learning Operations Coordinator role (MLH-026). My CV and cover letter are attached for your review. Thank you for considering my application.

Kind regards,
Dara Sok

Why this email works. The subject identifies who is applying and for which job. The body identifies the attachments and is short enough to scan. The signed cover letter carries the detailed case for the application.

Practice · Conduct a two-minute peer review

  1. Ask a partner to locate the strongest qualification in the top half of the CV.
  2. Ask them to underline the employer-specific reason in the cover letter.
  3. Check role names, dates and numbers across both documents together. Ask your partner to point to one claim that would benefit from more detail.
  4. Apply the feedback, reopen the files and note the version and submission date in your private tracker.

Check your work. If the vacancy asks for DOCX, upload DOCX even if you prefer the look of your PDF. If the preview breaks dates into the wrong fields, correct them in the portal and simplify the file’s layout for future applications.

title: Complete a tailored application
html:
Capstone · Produce a complete application

Choose a real vacancy or use the fictional Learning Operations Coordinator vacancy from Lesson 2. Spend about 50 minutes planning, writing and checking both documents. Work from your own facts if you choose a real job.

  1. Plan · 10 minutes. Capture the role, reference, and instructions. Map at least three requirements to evidence. Choose one verified reason for applying.
  2. Draft your CV · 15 minutes. Choose your section order, then draft three evidence bullets. Move your strongest evidence near the top. Use reverse chronology within sections.
  3. Draft your letter · 15 minutes. Identify the vacancy, connect a verified employer detail to your fit, explain one or two examples, and close courteously.
  4. Review · 10 minutes. Score both files using the rubric. Fix the two lowest-scoring items first. Compare files for consistency and check the final export.

Submit for review. Prepare the vacancy notes, evidence map, CV and cover letter. If you are sharing a practice submission with peers, remove real contact details and any sensitive information.

Score your work out of 20

Give each row a score from 0 to 4. A score of 0 means missing, 1 means unclear, 2 means partly done, 3 means clear with a minor revision, and 4 means ready.

CriterionWhat earns 4 points
Vacancy alignmentThree relevant requirements are mapped, and the strongest evidence appears early.
CV structureSections suit the role, entries are ordered consistently, and contact details are clear.
Evidence qualityBullets are specific, truthful, and grounded in actions, context, and results or purpose.
Letter structureThe opening is employer-specific, the body adds context, and the close is concise and courteous.
Final checksFacts agree across files, the export is readable, and the submission meets the advert’s requirements.

Review the example before scoring your own

Dara’s evidence matches the three essentials and the two body paragraphs develop distinct examples. The CV uses dates and names consistent with the letter. The sample contact information is a placeholder, so a real submission would still need a working phone number where required and a verified destination. This is a final-check issue even if the writing scores well.

Use your score to decide what to revise

17–20. Recheck the employer’s instructions and fix small issues. 12–16. Revise the lowest-scoring evidence or paragraph and score again. 0–11. Return to the evidence map and restructure the draft. Any inaccurate claim or missing required attachment must be fixed before submission, even with a high score.

quiz.prompt: What controls the final file type?

choices.c: A rule to always use PDF

quiz.feedback: Use the employer’s requested format. It takes priority over a general layout preference.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in an evidence map?

choices.b: A requirement, a verifiable example, and where to use it
choices.c: The same bullet for every role

quiz.feedback: Mapping requirements to proof helps you select which evidence belongs in the CV and which example deserves explanation in the letter.

quiz.prompt: When should education sit above experience?

choices.b: Only when the CV has two pages
choices.c: When a qualification is essential or your strongest relevant evidence

quiz.feedback: Section order should bring the most relevant proof forward. The dates within each section can still be reverse chronological.

quiz.prompt: Which bullet gives the recruiter the clearest proof?

choices.b: Checked weekly sign-in sheets and flagged missing entries before reporting

quiz.feedback: It identifies the action, record, timing, and purpose. A defensible outcome can be useful without a percentage.

quiz.prompt: Which opening is most specific to the role?

choices.a: I am applying for MLH-026. Your evening programme serves working adults, and I have coordinated class changes for six instructors.
choices.b: Please read my CV and let me know.

quiz.feedback: The opening identifies the vacancy, names a verified programme detail, and links experience to the employer’s needs.

quiz.prompt: What should a body paragraph add to the CV?

choices.a: A copy of the entire work history
choices.c: The situation, the action you took, and why it matters to the new role

quiz.feedback: Expanding a CV bullet helps the employer understand your contribution and how it transfers.

quiz.prompt: What can you check by pasting a PDF’s text into a plain-text editor?

choices.a: That every hiring system will score it highly
choices.b: Whether the text can be extracted in the expected order
choices.c: Whether the file is the requested type

quiz.feedback: The test gives you a basic reading-order check. Hiring systems differ, so also review any fields the portal fills automatically.

quiz.prompt: You spot a date that differs across your two exported files. What should you do?

choices.a: Verify the correct date, fix the source files, and reopen both exports
choices.b: Send them since the error is minor
choices.c: Remove all dates from the CV

quiz.feedback: Consistent dates help the employer place your evidence in context. Verify the fact and check the actual files after exporting.
